## 4.5.2 Bounding Type-2 Crossings

In this section we show that for every ordering \(\sigma\) of the auxiliary columns in L, \(\mathsf{cost}_2(\sigma)\le O(N^*\mathrm{logloglog}N^*)\). For the remainder of the section, we fix an ordering \(\sigma\) of L, and we denote the corresponding partitioning tree \(T(\sigma)\) by _T_. Recall that we have defined a set C of _N_ columns, so that \(|\mathcal{C}|,|\mathcal{L}|\le N\), and |_V(T_)|=_O(N_). It is then sufficient to prove the following theorem:

**Theorem 4.15** _For every vertex_ \(v\in V(T)\), \(\mathsf{cost}_2(v)\le O(\mathrm{log}N)+O(\mathsf{cost}_1(v))\).

Assuming that the theorem is correct, we get that \(\mathsf{cost}_2(\sigma)\le O(\mathsf{cost}_1(\sigma))+O(|V(T)|\cdot\mathrm{log}N)=O(N^*\mathrm{logloglog}N^*)+O(N\mathrm{log}N)=O(N^*\mathrm{logloglog}N^*)\).

The remainder of this subsection is dedicated to the proof of Theorem 4.15. We fix a vertex \(v\in V(T)\), and we denote _S=S(v_). We also let _L=L(v_) be the vertical line that _v_ owns. Our goal is to show that the number of type-2 crossings of _L_ is bounded by _O_(cost<sub>1</sub>(_v_))+_O_(log_N_).

Recall that instances _X_<sub>1</sub>_,...,X<sub>N</sub>_ are stacked on top of each other, so that the first log_N_ rows with integral coordinates belong to _X_<sub>1</sub>, the next log_N_ rows belong to _X_<sub>2</sub>, and so on. If we have a crossing \((p,p')\), where \(p\in X_s\) and \(p'\in X_{s^\prime}\), then we say that the instances _X<sub>s</sub>_ and \(X_{s^\prime}\) are _responsible_ for this crossings. Recall that \(p,p'\) may only define a crossing if they lie on opposite sides of the line _L_, and if no point of \(\hat{X}\) lies in the strip _S_ between the row of _p_ and the row of \(p'\). It is then clear that every instance _X<sub>s</sub>_ may be responsible for at most two type-2 crossings of _L_: one in which the second instance \(X_{s^\prime}\) responsible for the crossing has \(s'<s\), and one in which \(s'>s\).

We further partition the type-2 crossings into two sub-types. Consider a crossing \((p,p')\), and let \(X_s,X_{s^\prime}\) be the two instances that are responsible for it. If either of \(X_s,X_{s^\prime}\) contributes a type-1 crossing to the cost of _L_, then we say that \((p,p')\) is a type-(2a) crossing; otherwise it is a type-(2b) crossing. Clearly, the total number of type-(2a) crossings is bounded by _O_(cost<sub>1</sub>(_v_)). It is now sufficient to show that the total number of all type-(2b) crossings is bounded by _O_(log_N_).

Consider now some type-(2b) crossing \((p,p')\), and let _X<sub>s</sub>_ and \(X_{s^\prime}\) be the two instances that are responsible for it, with \(p\in X_s\). We assume that \(s<s'\). Since neither instance contributes a crossing to cost<sub>1</sub>(_v_), it must be the case that all points of \(X_s\cap S\) lie to the left of _L_ and all points of \(X_{s^\prime}\cap S\) lie to the right of _L_ or vice versa. Moreover, if \(s'>s+1\), then for all \(s<s''<s'\), \(X_{s^{\prime\prime}}\cap S=\emptyset\).

It would be convenient for us to collapse each of the instances _X_<sub>1</sub>_,...,X<sub>N</sub>_ into a single row. In order to do so, for each \(1\le s\le N\), we replace all rows on which the points of _X<sub>s</sub>_ lie with a single row _R<sub>s</sub>_. If some point of _X<sub>s</sub>_ lies on some column _C_, then we add a point at the intersection of _R<sub>s</sub>_ and _C_.

We say that a row _R<sub>s</sub>_ is _empty_ if there are no input points in \(R_s\cap S\). We say that it is a _neutral_ row, if there are points in \(R_s\cap S\) both to the left of _L_ and to the right of _L_. We say that it is a _left row_ if \(R_s\cap S\) only contains points lying to the left of _L_, and we say that it is a _right row_ if \(R_s\cap S\) only contains points lying to the right of _L_.

If we now consider any type-(2b) crossing \((p,p')\), and the instances \(X_s,X_{s^\prime}\) that are responsible for it, with \(s<s'\), then it must be the case that exactly one of the rows \(R_s,R_{s^\prime}\) is a left row, and the other is a right row. Moreover, if \(s'>s+1\), then every row lying between _R<sub>s</sub>_ and \(R_{s^\prime}\) is an empty row.

Let us denote the points in _X_<sub>1</sub> by _p_<sub>1</sub>_,...,p_log_N_, where for each \(1\le i\le logN\), point _p<sub>i</sub>_ lies in column _C_<sub>2_<sup>i</sup>_</sub>. In each subsequent instance _X_<sub>2</sub>_,X_<sub>3</sub>_,..._, the point is shifted by one unit to the right, so that in instance _X<sub>s</sub>_ it lies in column _C_<sub>2_<sup>i</sup>+s_-1</sub>; every column in C must contain exactly one copy of point _p<sub>i</sub>_.

Consider now all copies of the point _p<sub>i</sub>_ that lie in the strip _S_. Let R_<sub>i</sub>_ be the set of rows containing these copies. Then two cases are possible: either (i) R_<sub>i</sub>_ is a contiguous set of rows, and the copies of _p<sub>i</sub>_ appear on R_<sub>i</sub>_ diagonally as an increasing sequence (the _j_th row of R_<sub>i</sub>_ contains a copy of _p<sub>i</sub>_ that lies in the _j_th column of C in the strip _S_); or R_<sub>i</sub>_ consists of two consecutive sets of rows; the first set, that we denote by \(\mathcal{R}'_i\), contains _R_<sub>1</sub>, and the second set, that we denote by \(\mathcal{R}''_i\), contains the last row _R<sub>N</sub>_. The copies of the point _p<sub>i</sub>_ also appear diagonally in \(\mathcal{R}'_i\) and in \(\mathcal{R}''_i\); in \(\mathcal{R}''_i\) the first copy lies on the first column of C in _S_; in \(\mathcal{R}'_i\) the last copy lies on the last column of C in _S_ (see Figure 6).

Indeed, consider any type-(2b) crossing \((p,p')\) in which a copy of _p<sub>i</sub>_ participates. We assume that the row of _p_ lies below the row of \(p'\). Assume first that both _p_ and \(p'\) lie on rows of R_<sub>i</sub>_, and let \(R,R'\) be these two rows, with \(p\in R\), \(p'\in R'\). Recall that, in order for \((p,p')\) to define a crossing, all input points that lie on \(R\cap S\) must lie to the left of _L_, and all point points that lie on \(R'\cap S\) must lie to the right of _L_, or the other way around. It is easy to verify (see Figure 6) that one of two cases must happen: either _R_ contains a copy of _p<sub>i</sub>_ lying closest to _L_ on its left, and \(R'\) contains a copy of _p<sub>i</sub>_ lying closest to _L_ on its right; or _R_ is the last row of \(\mathcal{R}'_i\), and \(R'\) is the first row of \(\mathcal{R}''_i\). Therefore, only two such crossing, with \(R,R'\in\mathcal{R}_i\) are possible.

Assume now that \(R\in\mathcal{R}_i\) and \(R'\unknown\in\mathcal{R}_i\); recall that we assume that \(R'\) lies above _R_. In either case, at most one such crossing is possible.

Lastly, we assume that \(R\unknown\in\mathcal{R}_i\) and \(R'\in\mathcal{R}_i\). The analysis is symmetric; it is easy to see that at most one such crossing is possible.

We conclude that for each \(1\le i\le logN\), at most four type-(2b) crossings of the line _L_ may involve copies of _p<sub>i</sub>_, and so the total number of type-(2b) crossings of _L_ is bounded by _O_(log_N_).

To summarize, we have shown that for every ordering \(\sigma\) of the auxiliary columns in \(\mathcal{L},\mathsf{cost}_1(\sigma),\mathsf{cost}_2(\sigma)\le O(N^*logloglogN^*)\), and so \(\mathsf{WB}_\sigma(\hat{X})=O(N^*logloglogN^*)\). ## 5 Extensions of Wilber Bound

In this section we define two extensions of the strong Wilber bound and extend our negative results to one of these bounds. In subsection 5.1, we provide formal definitions of these bounds, and we present our negative result in subsequent subsections.

### 5.1 Definitions

Assume that we are given an input set _X_ of _n_ points, that is a permutation. Let L_<sup>V</sup>_ be the set of all vertical lines with half-integral _x_-coordinates between 1/2 and _n_-1/2, and let L_<sup>H</sup>_ be the set of all horizontal lines with half-integral _y_-coordinates between 1/2 and _n_-1/2. Recall that for every permutation \(\sigma\) of L_<sup>V</sup>_, we have defined a bound \(\mathsf{WB}_\sigma(X)\). We can similarly define a bound \(\mathsf{WB}'_{\sigma^\prime}(X)\) for every permutation \(\sigma'\) of L_<sup>H</sup>_. We also let \(\mathsf{WB}'(X)\) be the maximum, over all permutations \(\sigma'\) of L_<sup>H</sup>_, of \(\mathsf{WB}'_{\sigma^\prime}(X)\). Equivalently, let \(X'\) be an instance obtained from _X_ by rotating it by 90 degrees clockwise. Then \(\mathsf{WB}'(X)=\mathsf{WB}(X')\). We denote by _B_ a bounding box that contains all points of _X_.

#### 5.1.1 First Extension - Consistent Guillotine Bound

In this section we define the _consistent Guillotine Bound_, cGB(_X_). Let \(\sigma\) be any permutations of all lines in \(\mathcal{L}^V\cup\mathcal{L}^H\). We start from a bounding box _B_ containing all points of _X_ and maintain a partition P of the plane into rectangular regions, where initially P={_B_}. We process the lines in \(\mathcal{L}^V\cup\mathcal{L}^H\) according to their ordering in \(\sigma\). Consider an iteration when a line _L_ is processed. Let _P_<sub>1</sub>_,...,P<sub>k</sub>_ be all rectangular regions in P that intersect the line _L_. For each such region _P<sub>j</sub>_, let \(P'_j\) and \(P''_j\) be the two rectangular regions into which the line _L_ splits _P<sub>j</sub>_. We update P by replacing each region _P<sub>j</sub>_, for \(1\le j\le k\), with the regions \(P'_j\) and \(P''_j\). Once all lines in \(\mathcal{L}^V\cup\mathcal{L}^H\) are processed, we terminate the process.

This recursive partitioning procedure can be naturally associated with a partitioning tree \(T=T_\sigma\) that is defined as follows:

• Each vertex \(v\in V(T)\) is associated with a rectangular region _S(v_) of the plane. If _r_ is the root of _T_, then _S(r_)=_B_.<tbc>

• Each non-leaf vertex _v_ is associated with a line \(L(v)\in\mathcal{L}^H\cup\mathcal{L}^V\) that was used to partition _S(v_) into two sub-regions, \(S'\) and \(S''\). Vertex _v_ has two children _v_<sub>1</sub>_,v_<sub>2</sub> in _T_, with \(S(v_1)=S'\) and \(S(v_2)=S''\).<tbc>

• For each leaf node _v_, the region _S(v_) contains at most one point of _X_.

We now define the cost cost(_v_) of each node \(v\in V(T)\). If the region _S(v_) contains no points of _X_, or it contains a single point of _X_, then cost(_v_)=0. Otherwise, we define cost(_v_) in the same manner as before. Assume first that the line _L(v_) is vertical. Let _p_<sub>1</sub>_,...,p<sub>k</sub>_ be all points in \(X\cap S(v)\), indexed in the increasing order of their _y_-coordinates. A pair (_p<sub>j</sub>,p_<sub>_j_+1</sub>) of consecutive points forms a crossing of _L(v_) for _S(v_), if they lie on the opposite sides of _L(v_). We then let cost(_v_) be the number of such crossings.

When _L(v_) is a horizontal line, cost(_v_) is defined analogously: we index the points of \(X\cap S(v)\) in the increasing order of their _x_-coordinates. We then say that a consecutive pair of such points is a crossing iff they lie on opposite sides of _L(v_). We let cost(_v_) be the number of such crossings.

For a fixed ordering \(\sigma\) of the lines in \(\mathcal{L}^V\cup\mathcal{L}^H\), and the corresponding partition tree \(T=T(\sigma)\), we define \(\mathsf{cGB}_\sigma(X)=\sum_{v\in V(T)}\mathsf{cost}(v)\).

Lastly, we define the consistent Guillotine Bound for a point set _X_ that is a permutation to be the maximum, over all orderings \(\sigma\) of the lines in \(\mathcal{L}^V\cup\mathcal{L}^H\), of \(\mathsf{cGB}_\sigma(X)\).

In the following subsection we define an even stronger bound, that we call the _Guillotine bound_, and we show that for every point set _X_ that is a permutation, \(\mathsf{cGB}(X)\le\mathsf{GB}(X)\), and moreover that \(\mathsf{GB}(X)\le O(\mathsf{OPT}(X))\). It then follows that for every point set _X_ that is a permutation, \(\mathsf{cGB}(X)\le O(\mathsf{OPT}(X))\).

In subsequent subsections, we prove the following negative result for cGB, which extends the results of Theorem 1.1.

**Theorem 5.1** _For every integer_ \(n'\)_, there is an integer_ \(n\ge n'\)_, and a set X of points that is a permutation with_ |_X_|=_n, such that_ \(\mathsf{OPT}(X)\ge\Omega(nloglogn)\) _but_ \(\mathsf{cGB}(X)\le O(nlogloglogn)\).

The following lemma will be helpful in the proof of Theorem 5.1; recall that \(\mathsf{WB}'(X)\) is the basic Wilber Bound, where we cut via horizontal lines only.

**Lemma 5.2** _For every instance X that is a permutation,_ \(\mathsf{cGB}(X)\le\mathsf{WB}(X)+\mathsf{WB}'(X)\).

**Proof:** Let \(\sigma\) be a permutation of \(\mathcal{L}^V\cup\mathcal{L}^H\), such that \(\mathsf{cGB}(X)=\mathsf{cGB}_\sigma(X)\). Notice that \(\sigma\) naturally induces a permutation \(\sigma'\) of L_<sup>V</sup>_ and a permutation \(\sigma''\) of L_<sup>H</sup>_. We show that \(\mathsf{cGB}_\sigma(X)\le\mathsf{WB}_{\sigma^\prime}(X)+\mathsf{WB}'_{\sigma^{\prime\prime}}(X)\). In order to do so, it is enough to show that for every vertical line \(L\in\mathcal{L}^V\), the cost that is charged to _L_ in the bound \(\mathsf{cGB}_\sigma(X)\) is less than or equal to the cost that is charged to _L_ in the bound \(\mathsf{WB}_{\sigma^\prime}(X)\), and similarly, for every horizontal line \(L'\in\mathcal{L}^H\), the cost that is charged to \(L'\) in the bound \(\mathsf{cGB}_\sigma(X)\) is less than or equal to the cost that is charged to \(L'\) in the bound \(\mathsf{WB}'_{\sigma^{\prime\prime}}(X)\). We show the former; the proof of the latter is similar.

Consider any line \(L\in\mathcal{L}^V\). We let _T_ be the partitioning tree associated with \(\mathsf{cGB}_\sigma(X)\), just before line _L_ is processed, and we let \(T'\) be defined similarly for \(\mathsf{WB}_{\sigma^\prime}(X)\). Let \(v\in V(T')\) be the leaf vertex with \(L\subseteq S(v)\), and let _U_ be the set of all leaf vertices _u_ of the tree _T_ with \(S(u)\cap L\neq\emptyset\). Observe that the set of vertical lines that appear before _L_ in \(\sigma\) and \(\sigma'\) is identical. Therefore, \(S(v)=\bigcup_{u\in U}S(u)\). It is easy to verify that, for every vertex \(u\in U\), every crossing that contributes to cost(_u_) is also a crossing that is charged to the line _L_ in the strip _S(v_). Therefore, the total number of crossings of line _L_ in tree \(T'\) that contribute to \(\mathsf{WB}_{\sigma^\prime}(X)\) is greater than or equal to the number of crossings of the line _L_ that contribute to \(\mathsf{cGB}_\sigma(X)\).

To conclude, we get that \(\mathsf{cGB}(X)=\mathsf{cGB}_\sigma(X)\le\mathsf{WB}_{\sigma^\prime}(X)+\mathsf{WB}'_{\sigma^{\prime\prime}}(X)\le\mathsf{WB}(X)+\mathsf{WB}'(X)\). \(\square\)

## 5.1.2 Guillotine Bound

In this section, we define a second extension of Wilber Bound, that we call Guillotine Bound, and denote by GB. The bound is more convenient to define using a partitioning tree instead of a sequence of lines. Let _X_ be a point set which is a permutation.

We define a guillotine partition of a point set _X_, together with the corresponding partitioning tree _T_. As before, every node \(v\in V(T)\) of the partitioning tree _T_ is associated with a rectangular region _S(v_) of the plane. At the beginning, we add the root vertex _r_ to the tree _T_, and we let _S(r_)=_B_, where _B_ is the bounding box containing all points of _X_. We then iterate, as long as some leaf vertex _v_ of _T_ has \(S(v)\cap X\) containing more than one point. In each iteration, we select any such leaf vertex _v_, and we select an arbitrary vertical or horizontal line _L(v_), that is contained in _S(v_), and partitions _S(v_) into two rectangular regions, that we denote by \(S'\) and \(S''\), such that \(X\cap S',X\cap S''\neq\emptyset\). We then add two child vertices _v_<sub>1</sub>_,v_<sub>2</sub> to _v_, and set \(S(v_1)=S'\) and \(S(v_2)=S''\). Once every leaf vertex _v_ has \(|S(v)\cap X|=1\), we terminate the process and obtain the final partitioning tree _T_.

The cost cost(_v_) of every vertex \(v\in V(T)\) is calculated exactly as before. We then let \(\mathsf{GB}_T(X)=\sum_{v\in V(T)}\mathsf{cost}(v)\), and we let GB(_X_) be the maximum, over all partitioning trees _T_, of GB_<sub>T</sub>(X_).

We note that the main difference between cGB(_X_) and GB(_X_) is that in cGB bound, the partitioning lines must be chosen consistently across all regions: that is, we choose a vertical or a horizontal line _L_ that crosses the entire bounding box _B_, and then we partition every region that intersects _L_ by this line _L_. In contrast, in the GB bound, we can partition each region _S(v_) individually, and choose different partitioning lines for different regions. It is then easy to see that GB is more general than cGB, and, in particular, for every point set _X_ that is a permutation, \(\mathsf{cGB}(X)\le\mathsf{GB}(X)\).

Lastly, we show that GB is a lower bound on the optimal solution cost, in the following lemma whose proof is deferred to Section D of Appendix.

**Lemma 5.3** _For any point set X that is a permutation,_ \(\mathsf{GB}(X)\le 2\mathsf{OPT}(X)\).

## 6 The Algorithms

In this section we provide the proof of Theorem 1.3. Both the polynomial time and the sub- exponential time algorithms follow the same framework. We start with a high-level overview of this framework. For simplicity, assume that the number of active columns in the input instance _X_ is an integral power of 2. The key idea is to decompose the input instance into smaller sub-instances, using the split instances defined in Section 3.1. We solve the resulting instances recursively and then combine the resulting solutions.

Suppose we are given an input point set _X_ that is a semi-permutation, with |_X_|=_m_, such that the number of active columns is _n_. We consider a _balanced_ partitioning tree _T_, where for every vertex \(v\in V(T)\), the line _L(v_) that _v_ owns splits the strip _S(v_) in the middle, with respect to the active columns that are contained in _S(v_). Therefore, the height of the partitioning tree is log_n_.

Consider now the set _U_ of vertices of _T_ that lie in the middle layer of _T_. We consider the split of (_X,T_) at _U_, obtaining a new collection of instances \((X^c,\{X_i^s\})_{i=1}^k\) where \(k=\Theta(\sqrt{n})\). Note that each resulting strip instance \(X_i^s\) contains \(\Theta(\sqrt{n})\) active columns, and so does the compressed instance _X<sup>c</sup>_.

We will recursively solve each such instance and then combine the resulting solutions. The key in the algorithm and its analysis is to show that there is a collection _Z_ of _O_(|_X_|) points, such that, if we are given any solution _Y<sup>c</sup>_ to instance _X<sup>c</sup>_, and, for all \(1\le i\le k\), any solution _Y<sub>i</sub>_ to instance \(X_i^s\), then \(Z\cup Y^c\cup\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^NY_i\right)\) is a feasible solution to instance _X_. Additionally, we show that the total number of input points that appear in all instances that participate in the same recursive level is bounded by _O_(OPT(_X_)). This ensures that in every recursive level we add at most _O_(OPT(_X_)) points to the solution, and the total solution cost is at most _O_(OPT(_X_)) times the number of the recursive levels, which is in turn bounded by _O_(loglog_n_).

In order to obtain the sub-exponential time algorithm, we restrict the recursion to _D_ levels, and then solve each resulting instance directly in time _r(X)c(X_)<sup>_O(c(X_))</sup> (recall that _r(X_) and _c(X_) are the number of active rows and active columns in instance _X_, respectively). Altogether, this approach gives an _O(D_)-approximation algorithm with running time at most \(\mathrm{poly}(m)\cdot\mathrm{exp}\left(n^{1/2^{\Omega(D)}}\mathrm{log}n\right)\) as desired. We now provide a formal definition of the algorithm and its analysis. In the remainder of this section, all logarithms are to the base of 2.

## 6.1 Special Solutions

Our algorithm will produce feasible solutions of a special form, that we call _special solutions_. Recall that, given a semi-permutation point set _X_, the auxiliary columns for _X_ are a set L of vertical lines with half-integral coordinates. We say that a solution _Y_ for _X_ is _special_ iff every point of _Y_ lies on an row that is active for _X_, and on a column of L. In particular, special solutions are by definition non-canonical (see Figure 7 for an illustration). The main advantage of the special solutions is that they allow us to easily use the divide-and-conquer approach.

**Observation 6.1** _There is an algorithm, that, given a set X of points that is a semi-permutation, and a canonical solution Y for X, computes a special solution_ \(Y'\) _for X, such that_ \(|Y'|\le 2|X|+2|Y|\)_. The running time of the algorithm is O_(|_X_|+|_Y_|).

**Proof:** We construct \(Y'\) as follows: For each point \(p\in X\cup Y\) , we add two points, \(p'\) and \(p''\) to \(Y'\), whose _y_-coordinate is the same as that of _p_, such that \(p'\) and \(p''\) lie on the lines of L appearing immediately to the left and immediately to the right of _p_, respectively. It is easy to verify that \(|Y'|=2|X|+2|Y|\).

We now verify that \(X\cup Y'\) is a feasible set of points. Consider two points _p,q_ in \(X\cup Y'\), such that _p.x\<q.x_. Notice that _p_ is either an original point in _X_ or it is a copy of some point \(\hat{p}\in X\cup Y\) . If \(p\in X\) or \(p=\hat{p}'\) for \(\hat{p}\in X\cup Y\) , then the point \(\hat{p}''\) lies in the rectangle \(\square_{p,q}\). Therefore, we can assume that \(p=\hat{p}''\) for some point \(\hat{p}\in X\cup Y\) .

Using a similar reasoning, we can assume that \(q=\hat{q}'\) for some point \(\hat{q}\in X\cup Y\) . Since \(X\cup Y\) is a satisfied point set, there must be a point \(r\in X\cup Y\) that lies in the rectangle \(\square_{\hat{p},\hat{q}}\). Moreover, from Observation 2.3, we can choose _r_ such that either \(r.x=\hat{p}.x\) or \(r.y=\hat{p}.y\). In either case, point \(r''\) also lies in \(\square_{\hat{p}^{\prime\prime},\hat{q}^\prime}=\square_{p,q}\), so (_p,q_) is satisfied by \(X\cup Y'\). Therefore, \(X\cup Y'\) is a feasible set of points. It is easy to see that \(Y'\) is a special solution. \(\square\)

<tbc>If \(\sigma\) is any ordering of the auxiliary columns in L, and \(T=T_\sigma\) is the corresponding partitioning tree, then any point set _Y_ that is a special solution for _X_ is also called a _T-special solution_ (although the notion of the solution _Y_ being special does not depend on the tree _T_, this notion will be useful for us later; in particular, a convenient way of thinking of a _T_-special solution is that every point of _Y_ must lie on an active row of _X_, and on a column that serves as a boundary for some strip _S(v_), where \(v\in V(T)\).)

## 6.2 Redundant Points and Reduced Point Sets

We say that a semi-permutation _X_ is in the _reduced form_ if there are no redundant points in _X_; in other words, if _p_<sub>_i_-1</sub>_,p<sub>i</sub>,p_<sub>_i_+1</sub> are three points lying on three consecutive active rows, then their _x_-coordinates are not all equal. **Lemma 6.5** _Let X be a point set that is a semi-permutation in reduced form. Then_ \(\mathsf{OPT}(X)\ge|X|/4-1\).

Moreover, since all points of _X_ lie on distinct rows, and each such point belongs to at most one pair in \(\Pi''\), for \(i\neq j\), \(y_i\neq y_j\). Therefore, \(|Y|\ge|\Pi''|\ge n/4-1\). □

## 6.3 The Algorithm Description

Suppose we are given an input set _X_ of points that is a semi-permutation. Let _T_ be any partitioning tree for _X_. We say that _T_ is a _balanced_ partitioning tree for _X_ iff for every non-leaf vertex \(v\in V(T)\) the following holds. Let \(v'\) and \(v''\) be the children of _v_ in the tree _T_. Let \(X'\) be the set of all input points lying in strip _S(v_), and let \(X'',X'''\) be defined similarly for \(S(v')\) and \(S(v'')\). Let _c_ be the number of active columns in instance \(X'\), and let \(c'\) and \(c''\) be defined similarly for \(X''\) and \(X'''\). Then we require that \(c',c''\le\lceil c/2\rceil\).

Given a partitioning tree _T_, we denote by \(\Lambda_i\) the set of all vertices of _T_ that lie in the _i_th _layer_ of _T_ - that is, the vertices whose distance from the root of _T_ is _i_ (so the root belongs to \(\Lambda_0\)). The<tbc>

<tbc>_height_ of the tree _T_, denoted by height(_T_), is the largest index _i_ such that \(\Lambda_i\neq\emptyset\). If the height of the tree _T_ is _h_, then we call the set \(\Lambda_{\lceil h/2\rceil}\) of vertices the _middle layer_ of _T_. Notice that, if _T_ is a balanced partitioning tree for input _X_, then its height is at most 2log_c(X_).

Our algorithm takes as input a set _X_ of points that is a semi-permutation, a balanced partition tree _T_ for _X_, and an integral parameter \(\rho>0\).

Intuitively, the algorithm uses the splitting operation to partition the instance _X_ into subinstances that are then solved recursively, until it obtains a collection of instances whose corresponding partitioning trees have height at most \(\rho\). We then either employ dynamic programming, or use a trivial _O_(log_c(X_))-approximation algorithm. The algorithm returns a special feasible solution for the instance. Recall that the height of the tree _T_ is bounded by \(2logc(X)\le 2logn\).

The following two theorems will be used as the recursion basis.

**Theorem 6.6** _There is an algorithm called_ LeafBST-1 _that, given a semi-permutation instance X of_ Min-Sat _in reduced form, and a partitioning tree T for it, produces a feasible T-special solution for X of cost at most_ 2|_X_|+2OPT(_X), in time_ \(|X|^{O(1)}\cdot c(X)^{O(c(X))}\).

**Theorem 6.7** _There is an algorithm called_ LeafBST-2 _that, given a semi-permutation instance X of_ Min-Sat _in reduced form, and a partitioning tree T for it, produces a feasible T-special solution of cost at most_ 2|_X_|height(_T), in time_ poly(|_X_|).

The proofs of both theorems are deferred to the next two subsections, after we complete the proof of Theorem 1.3 using them. We now provide a schematic description of our algorithm. Depending on the guarantees that we would like to achieve, whenever the algorithm calls procedure LeafBST, it will call either procedure LeafBST-1 or procedure LeafBST-2; we specify this later.

\(\text{RecursiveBST}(X,T,\rho)\)

1. Keep removing redundant points from _X_ until _X_ is in reduced form.<tbc>

2. IF _T_ has height at most \(\rho\),<tbc>

3. **return** LeafBST(_X,T_)<tbc>

4. Let _U_ be the set of vertices lying in the middle middle layer of _T_.<tbc>

5. Compute the split \((X^c,\{X_v^s\}_{v\in U})\) of (_X,T_) at _U_.<tbc>

6. Compute the corresponding sub-trees \((T^c,\{T_v^s\}_{v\in U})\) of _T_.<tbc>

7. For each vertex \(v\in U\), call to RecursiveBST with input \((X_v^s,T_v^s,\rho)\), and let _Y<sub>v</sub>_ be the solution returned by it.<tbc>

8. Call RecursiveBST with input \((X^c,T^c,\rho)\), and let \(\hat{Y}\) be the solution returned by it.<tbc>

9. Let _Z_ be a point set containing, for each vertex \(v\in U\), for each point \(p\in X_v^s\), two copies \(p'\) and \(p''\) of _p_ with \(p'.y=p''.y=p.y\), where \(p'\) lies on the left boundary of _S(v_), and \(p''\) lies on the right boundary of _S(v_).<tbc>

10. **return** \(Y^*=Z\cup\hat{Y}\cup(\bigcup_{v\in U}Y_v)\)

## 6.4 Analysis

We start by showing that the solution that the algorithm returns is _T_-special.

**Observation 6.8** _Assuming that_ LeafBST(_X,T_) _returns a T-special solution, the solution Y_<sup>∗</sup> _returned by Algorithm_ RecursiveBST\((X,T,\rho)\) _is a T-special solution._

**Proof:** The proof is by induction on the recursion depth. The base of the induction is the calls to Procedure LeafBST(_X,T_), which return _T_-special solutions by our assumption.

Consider now some call to Algorithm RecursiveBST\((X,T,\rho)\). From the induction hypothesis, the resulting solution \(\hat{Y}\) for instance _X<sup>c</sup>_ is _T<sup>c</sup>_-special, and, for every vertex \(v\in U\), the resulting solution _Y<sub>v</sub>_ for instance \(X_v^s\) is _T<sub>v</sub>_-special. Since both _T<sup>c</sup>_ and every tree \(\{T_v\}_{v\in U}\) are subtrees of _T_, and since the points of _Z_ lie on boundaries of strips in \(\{S(v)\}_{v\in U}\), the final solution _Y_<sup>∗</sup> is _T_-special. \(\square\)

We next turn to prove that the solution _Y_<sup>∗</sup> computed by Algorithm RecursiveBST\((X,T,\rho)\) is feasible. In order to do so, we will use the following immediate observation.

**Observation 6.9** _Let Y_<sup>∗</sup> _be the solution returned by Algorithm_ RecursiveBST\((X,T,\rho)\)_, and let_ \(u\in U\) _be any vertex. Then:_

• _Any point_ \(y\in Y^*\) _that lies in the interior of S(u_) _must lie on an active row of instance_ \(X_u^s\).<tbc>

• _Any point_ \(y\in Y^*\) _that lies on the boundary of S(u_) _must belong to in_ \(\hat{Y}\cup Z\)_. Moreover, the points of_ \(\hat{Y}\cup Z\) _may not lie in the interior of S(u)._<tbc>

• _If R is an active row for instance_ \(X_u^s\)_, then set Z contains two points, lying on the intersection of R with the left and the right boundaries of S(u), respectively._

We are now ready to prove that the algorithm returns feasible solutions. In the following proof, when we say that a row _R_ is an active row of strip _S(u_), we mean that some point of instance \(X_v^s\) lies on row _R_, or equivalently, _R_ is an active row for instance \(X_v^s\).

**Theorem 6.10** _Assume that the recursive calls to Algorithm_ RecursiveBST _return a feasible special solution_ \(\hat{Y}\) _for instance X<sup>c</sup>, and for each_ \(v\in U\)_, a feasible special solution Y<sub>v</sub> for the strip instance_ \(X_v^s\)_. Then the point set_ \(Y^*=Z\cup\hat{Y}\cup(\bigcup_{v\in U}Y_v)\) _is a feasible solution for instance X._

**Proof:** It would be convenient for us to consider the set of all points in \(X^c\cup X\cup Y^*\) simultaneously. In order to do so, we start with the set \(X\cup Y^*\) of points. For every vertex \(v\in U\), we select an arbitrary active column _C<sub>v</sub>_ in strip _S(v_), and we then add a copy of every point \(p\in X_v^s\) to column _C<sub>v</sub>_. The resulting set of points, obtained after processing all strips _S(v_) is identical to the set _X<sup>c</sup>_ of points (except possibly for horizontal spacing between active columns), and we do not distinguish between them.

Consider any pair of points _p,q_ that lie in \(Y^*\cup X\), which are not collinear. Our goal is to prove that some point \(r\neq p,q\) with \(r\in X\cup Y^*\) lies in \(\square_{p,q}\). We assume w.l.o.g. that _p_ lies to the left of _q_. We also assume that _p.y\<q.y_ (that is, point _p_ is below point _q_); the other case is symmetric.

Assume first that at least one of the two points (say _p_) lies in the interior of a strip _S(u_), for some \(u\in U\). We then consider two cases. First, if _q_ also lies in the interior of the same strip, then<tbc>

<tbc>\(p,q\in X_u^s\cup Y_u\), and, since we have assumed that _Y<sub>u</sub>_ is a feasible solution for instance \(X_u^s\), the two points are satisfied in \(X_u^s\cup Y_u\), and hence in \(X\cup Y^*\). Otherwise, _q_ does not lie in the interior of strip _S(u_). Then, from Observation 6.9, if _R_ is the row on which point _p_ lies, then _R_ is an active row for instance \(X_u^s\), and the point that lies on the intersection of the row _R_ and the right boundary of strip _S(u_) was added to _Z_. Therefore, we can now assume that both _p_ and _q_ lie on boundaries of strips \(\{S(u)|u\in U\}\). Since every pair of consecutive strips share a boundary, and since, from the above assumptions, _p_ lies to the left of _q_, we can choose the strips _S(u_) and _S(v_), such that _p_ lies on the left boundary of _S(u_), and _q_ lies on the right boundary of _S(v_). Notice that, if _p_ lies on a row that is active for strip _S(u_), then a point that lies on the same row and belongs to the right boundary of the strip _S(u_) has been added to _Z_; this point satisfies the pair (_p,q_). ## 6.5.1 Conflicting sets

Our algorithm uses the notion of conflicting point sets, defined as follows.

**Definition 6.14 (Conflicting Sets)** _Let Z and_ \(Z'\) _be sets of points. We say that Z and_ \(Z'\) _are_ conflicting _if there is a pair of points_ \(p\in Z\) _and_ \(p'\in Z'\)_, such that_ \((p,p')\) _is not satisfied in_ \(Z\cup Z'\)_. In other words, set_ \(Z\cup Z'\) _contains no point in_ \(\square_{p,p^\prime}\backslash\{p,p'\}\).

**Lemma 6.15** _Let Z and_ \(Z'\) _be two point sets, each of which is a satisfied set. Then the sets Z and_ \(Z'\) _are not conflicting if and only if_ \(Z\cup Z'\) _is satisfied._

**Proof:** Assume first that \(Z\cup Z'\) is satisfied. Then it is clear that for every pair \(p\in Z\), \(p'\in Z'\) of points, some point \(r\in Z\cup Z'\) lies in \(\square_{p,p^\prime}\backslash\{p,p'\}\)), so _Z_ and \(Z'\) are not conflicting.

Assume now that _Z_ and \(Z'\) are conflicting, and let \(p\in Z\) and \(p'\in Z'\) be the corresponding pair of points. Then \((p,p')\) is not satisfied in \(Z\cup Z'\), and so \(Z\cup Z'\) is not a satisfied set of points. \(\square\)

The following definition is central to our algorithm.

**Definition 6.16 (Top representation)** _Let Z be any set of points. A_ top representation _of Z, that we denote by_ top(_Z), is a subset_ \(Z'\subseteq Z\) _of points, obtained as follows: for every column C that contains points from Z, we add the topmost point of Z that lies on C to_ \(Z'\).

**Observation 6.17** _Let_ \(\mathrm{top}(Z)\subseteq Z\) _be the top representation of Z, and let R be a row lying strictly above all points in Z. Let Y be any set of points lying on row R. Then top(Z_) _is conflicting with Y if and only if Z is conflicting with Y ._

**Proof:** Assume that _Y_ is conflicting with _Z_, and let \(p\in Y\) , \(q\in Z\) be a pair of points, such that no point of \(Y\cup Z\) lies in \(\square_{p,q}\backslash\{p,q\}\). But then \(q\in\mathrm{top}(Z)\) must hold, and no point of \(\mathrm{top}(Z)\cup Y\) lies in \(\square_{p,q}\backslash\{p,q\}\), so top(_Z_) and _Y_ are conflicting.

Assume now that top(_Z_) and _Y_ are conflicting, and let \(p\in Y\) , \(q\in\mathrm{top}(Z)\) be a pair of points, such that no point of \(Y\cup\mathrm{top}(Z)\) lies in \(\square_{p,q}\backslash\{p,q\}\). But then no point of \(Y\cup Z\) lies in \(\square_{p,q}\backslash\{p,q\}\), and, since \(\mathrm{top}(Z)\subseteq Z\), sets top(_Z_) and _Y_ are conflicting. \(\square\)

For each box \(B'\in\mathcal{B}(T')\), the lowest and the highest rows containing points of \(B'\) are denoted by \(\text{first}(B')\) and \(\text{last}(B')\) respectively.

## Projections of points:

Recall that the solution that our recursive algorithm returns is _T_-special, that is, the points that participate in the solution lie on the active rows of _X_ and on _T_-auxiliary columns. Let _Y_ be a feasible solution obtained by our algorithm RecursiveBST(_X_, _T_, \(\rho\)), where \(\rho=1\). Notice the every point in _Y_ is obtained by "projecting" some input point \(p\in X\) to the boundary of some strip _S(v_) for \(v\in V(T)\), where strip _S(v_) contains _p_. For each point \(p\in X\) and node \(v\in V(T)\) of the partitioning tree, such that \(p\in S(v)\), we define the set proj(_p,v_) to contain two points on the same row as _p_, that lie on the left and right boundaries of _S(v_), respectively. We denote by _Y<sub>p,v</sub>_ the set that contain the two points proj(_p,v_) if our algorithm adds these two points to the solution. Notice that, since all points of _X_ lie on distinct rows, for any two points \(p\neq p'\), for any pair \(v,v'\in V(T)\) of vertices, \(\mathsf{proj}(p,v)\cap\mathsf{proj}(p',v')=\emptyset\). Observe that we can now write the solution _Y_ as \(Y=\bigcup_{p\in X}\bigcup_{v\in V(T)}Y_{p,v}\). The following lemma characterizes the points of _Y_ in terms of boxes.

**Lemma 7.2** _For every point_ \(p\in X\) _and every node_ \(v\in V(T)\) _of the partitioning tree,_ |_Y<sub>p,v</sub>_|=2 _if and only if there is an index_ \(1\le i\le D\)_, and a subtree_ \(T'\in\mathcal{T}_i\)_, such that (i) p is the first or the last point of its_ \(T'\)_-box; (ii) v lies in the middle layer of_ \(T'\)_; and (iii) S(v_) _contains p._

**Proof:** Let \(1\le i\le D\) be an index, and let \(T'\in\mathcal{T}_i\) be the corresponding partitioning tree. We denote the corresponding point set by \(X'\). Let _v_<sub>1</sub>_,...,v<sub>k</sub>_ be the leaf vertices of \(T'\), and let _u_<sub>1</sub>_,...,u<sub>r</sub>_ be the vertices lying in the middle layer of \(T'\). The only points added to the solution when instance \(X'\) is processed are the following: for every \(1\le j\le r\), for every point \(p\in X'\cap S(u_j)\), we add the two copies of _p_ to the boundaries of _S(u<sub>j</sub>_). In subsequent, or in previous iterations, we may add points to boundaries of _S(u<sub>j</sub>_), but we will never add two copies of the same input point to both boundaries of _S(u<sub>j</sub>_). Therefore, if |_Y<sub>p,v</sub>_|=2, then there must be an index _i_, and a tree \(T'\in\mathcal{T}_i\), such that _v_ lies in the middle layer of \(T'\), and _S(v_) contains _p_. Observe that for every \(T'\)-box _B_, instance \(X'\) only contains the first and the last point of _B_; all remaining points are redundant for \(X'\), and such points are not projected to the boundaries of their strips. Therefore, _p_ must be the first or the last point of its \(T'\)-box. \(\square\)

## An equivalent view of our algorithm:

We can think of our algorithm as follows. First, we compute all families T<sub>0</sub>,T<sub>1</sub>_,...,_T_<sub>D</sub>_ of trees, and for each tree \(T'\) in each family T_<sub>i</sub>_, all \(T'\)-boxes.<tbc>

For each point \(p\in X\), for each vertex \(v\in V(T)\) of the partitioning tree _T_, such that \(p\in S(v)\), we add the projection points proj(_p,v_) to the solution, depending on whether there exists an index \(i\in\{0,1,\dots,D\}\) and a tree \(T'\in\mathcal{T}_i\), such that _v_ lies in the middle layer \(U_{T^\prime}\) of \(T'\), and whether _p_ is the first or last point of its \(T'\)-box. Notice that in the online setting, when the point _p_ arrives, we need to be able to immediately decide which copies of _p_ to add to the solution. Since the trees in the families T<sub>0</sub>,T<sub>1</sub>_,...,_T_<sub>D</sub>_ are known in advance, and we discover, for every vertex \(v\in V(T)\) whether \(p\in S(v)\) immediately when _p_ arrives, the only missing information, for every relevant tree \(T'\), is whether vertex _p_ is the first or the last vertex in its \(T'\)-box. In fact it is easy to check whether it is the first vertex in its \(T'\)-box, but we will not discover whether it is the last vertex in its \(T'\)-box until the next iteration, at which point it is too late to add points to the solution that lie in the row of _p_.

In order to avoid this difficulty, we slightly modify the instance and the solution.

## 7.2 Online-friendly solutions

In this section we slightly modify both the input set of points and the solutions produced by our algorithm, in order to adapt them to the online setting.

### Modifying the Instance.

Let _X_={_p_<sub>1</sub>_,...,p<sub>m</sub>_} be the input set of points, where for all \(1\le i\le m\), the _y_-coordinate of _p<sub>i</sub>_ is _i_. We produce a new instance \(X'=\{p'_i,p''_i|1\le i\le m\}\), as follows: for all \(1\le i\le m\), we let \(p'_i\) and \(p''_i\) be points whose _y_-coordinates are (2_i_-1) and 2_i_, respectively, and whose _x_-coordinate is the same as that of _p<sub>i</sub>_. We refer to \(p'_i\) and to \(p''_i\) as _copies of p<sub>i</sub>_.

Clearly, \(|X'|=2|X|\), and it is easy to verify that \(\mathsf{OPT}(X')\le 2\mathsf{OPT}(X)\). Indeed, if we let _Y_ be a solution for _X_, we can construct a solution \(Y'\) for \(X'\), by creating, for every point \(q\in Y\) , two copies \(q'\) and \(q''\), that are added to rows with _y_-coordinates 2_q.y_-1 and 2_q.y_ respectively.

For convenience, we denote \(\mathcal{T}=\bigcup_{i=0}^D\mathcal{T}_i\). Notice that, for every tree \(T'\in\mathcal{T}\) , for every point _p<sub>i</sub>_ of the original input _X_, copy \(p'_i\) of _p<sub>i</sub>_ may never serve as the last point of a \(T'\)-box, and copy \(p''_i\) of _p<sub>i</sub>_ may never serve as the first point of a \(T'\)-box.

### Modifying the Solution.

Let _Y_ be the solution that our _O_(loglog_n_)-approximation algorithm produces for the new instance \(X'\). For convenience, for all \(1\le i\le 2m\), we denote by _R<sub>i</sub>_ the row with _y_-coordinate _i_. Notice that all points of _Y_ lying on a row _R_<sub>2_i_-1</sub> are projections of the point \(p'_i\). Since this point may only serve as the first point of a \(T'\)-box for every tree \(T'\in\mathcal{T}\) , when point \(p'_i\) arrives online, we can immediately compute all projections of \(p'_i\) that need to be added to the solution. All points of _Y_ lying on row _R_<sub>2_i_</sub> are projections of the point \(p''_i\). This point may only serve as the last point of a \(T'\)-box in a tree \(T'\in\mathcal{T}\) . But we cannot know whether \(p''_i\) is the last point in its \(T'\)-box until we see the next input point. Motivated by these observations, we now modify the solution _Y_ as follows.

We perform _m_ iterations. In iteration _i_, we consider the row _R_<sub>2_i_</sub>. If no point of _Y_ lies on row _R_<sub>2_i_</sub>, then we continue to the next iteration. Otherwise, we move every point of _Y_ that lies on row _R_<sub>2_i_</sub> to row _R_<sub>2_i_+1</sub> (that is, one row up). Additionally, we add another copy \(p'''_i\) of point _p<sub>i</sub>_ to row _R_<sub>2_i_</sub>, while preserving its _x_-coordinate.

In order to show that the resulting solution is a feasible solution to instance \(X'\), it is sufficient to show that the solution remains feasible after every iteration. Let _Y<sub>i</sub>_ be the solution _Y_ obtained<tbc>

before the _i_th iteration, and let \(S_i=X'\cup Y_i\). We can obtain the new solution _Y_<sub>_i_+1</sub> equivalently as follows. First, we collapse the rows _R_<sub>2_i_+1</sub> and _R_<sub>2_i_</sub> for the set _S<sub>i</sub>_ of points into the row _R_<sub>2_i_+1</sub>, obtaining a new set \(S'_i\) of points that is guaranteed to be satisfied. Notice that now both row _R_<sub>2_i_+1</sub> and row _R_<sub>2_i_-1</sub> contain a point at _x_-coordinate (_p<sub>i</sub>).x_, while row _R_<sub>2_i_</sub> contains no points. Therefore, if we add to \(S'_i\) a point with _x_-coordinate (_p<sub>i</sub>).x_, that lies at row _R_<sub>2_i_</sub>, then the resulting set of points, that we denote by _S_<sub>_i_+1</sub> remains satisfied. But it is easy to verify that \(S_{i+1}=X'\cup Y_{i+1}\), where _Y_<sub>_i_+1</sub> is the solution obtained after iteration _i_. We denote by \(Y'\) the final solution obtained by this transformation of _Y_ . It is easy to see that \(|Y'|\le 2|Y|\le O(loglogn)\mathsf{OPT}(X)\).

### 7.3 The Final Online Algorithm

We now provide the final online algorithm, that is described in two steps.

First, we assume that in the online sequence, all input points are doubled, that is, for \(1\le i\le m\), both in iterations (2_i_-1) and 2_i_ the algorithm receives copies of the input point _p<sub>i</sub>_; the point received at iteration (2_i_-1) is denoted by \(p'_i\), and the point received at iteration 2_i_ is denoted by \(p''_i\). The algorithm computes the collection T of trees at the beginning. When a point \(p'_i\) arrives, we can identify, for every tree \(T'\in\mathcal{T}\) , whether \(p'_i\) is the first point in any \(T'\)-box. We then add projections of the point \(p'_i\) to the corresponding strips _S(v_) as needed, all on row _R_<sub>2_i_-1</sub>. When a point \(p''_i\) arrives, we only discover whether it is the last point of any \(T'\)-box, for all \(T'\in\mathcal{T}\) , in the following iteration. Therefore, in iteration 2_i_+1, we add both the copy \(p''_i\) of \(p''_i\), and all its relevant projections, to row _R_<sub>2_i_+1</sub>. Note that at the same time, we may also add projections of point \(p'_{i+1}\) to row _R_<sub>2_i_+1</sub>. It is easy to verify that the resulting solution is precisely \(Y'\), and therefore it is a feasible solution. The cost of the solution is bounded by \(O(loglogn)\cdot\mathsf{OPT}(X)\).

Lastly, for all \(1\le i\le m\), we unify the iterations (2_i_-1) and (2_i_) into a single iteration in a straightforward way.

## B Binary Search Trees and Equivalence with the Geometric tion

We start by formally defining the BST model. An _access sequence X_={_x_<sub>1</sub>_,...,x<sub>m</sub>_} is a sequence of keys from the universe {1_,...,n_}. We consider algorithms that maintain a Binary Search Tree (BST) _T_ over the set {1_,...,n_} of keys, and support only _access_ operations. After each access the algorithm can reconfigure the tree _T_, as follows. (The definitions below are adapted from \[DHI<sup>+</sup>09\].)

**Definition B.1** _Given two BST’s T_<sub>1</sub> _and T_<sub>2</sub>_, a subtree_ \(\tau\) _of T_<sub>1</sub> _containing the root of T_<sub>1</sub>_, and a tree_ \(\tau'\) _with_ \(V(\tau)=V(\tau')\)_, we say that T_<sub>2</sub> _is a_ reconfiguration of _T_<sub>1</sub> via the operation \(\tau\rightarrow\tau'\)_, if T_<sub>2</sub> _is identical to T_<sub>1</sub> _except that_ \(\tau\) _is replaced by_ \(\tau'\)_. The_ cost _of the reconfiguration is_ \(|V(\tau)|\).

**Definition B.2** _Given an access sequence X_=(_x_<sub>1</sub>_,x_<sub>2</sub>_,...,x<sub>m</sub>), an_ execution sequence _of a BST algorithm on X is_ \(E=(T_0,\tau_1\rightarrow\tau'_1,\dots,\tau_m\rightarrow\tau'_m)\)_, where T_<sub>0</sub> _is the initial tree, and for each_ \(1\le i\le m\), \(\tau_i\rightarrow\tau_{i+1}\) _is a valid reconfiguration operation to be executed at step i, such that_ \(x_i\in\tau_i\)_. The cost of execution E is_ \(\sum_{i=1}^m|V(\tau_i)|\).

As stated in \[DHI<sup>+</sup>09\], the cost of an algorithm’s execution in this model is identical to within a constant-factor to other standard models. This includes, for example, the model that we informally defined in the introduction, where, after each access, the tree is modified by a series of rotations, and the cost consists of the number of such rotations and the distance of the accessed key from the tree’s root.

The BST problem can now be defined as follows:

**Problem B.3 (The BST problem)** _Given an access sequence X, compute an execution sequence for X that has minimum cost. In the online version, the t-th element of the sequence X is revealed at time t, and we need to output a valid reconfiguration operation_ \(\tau_t\rightarrow\tau'_t\) _with_ \(x_t\in\tau_t\) _before the_ (_t_+1)_-th element is revealed._

Observe that any access sequence _X_ uniquely corresponds to a set _P_ of points in the plane that is a semi-permutation: if we denote _X_=(_x_<sub>1</sub>_,x_<sub>2</sub>_,...,x<sub>m</sub>_), then for each \(1\le i\le m\), we add the point (_x<sub>i</sub>,i_) to _P_. For convenience, we do not distinguish between the input sequence _X_ and the corresponding set _P_ of points.

**Theorem B.4 (Implied by Lemmas 2.1, 2.2 and 2.3 from \[DHI<sup>+</sup>09\])** _There is an (online) algorithm for BST, that, for any access sequence X computes an execution sequence of cost at most O_(|_X_|+_c(X_))_, if and only if there is an (online) algorithm for the_ Min-Sat _problem, that, given any input X, computes a solution Y of cost_ \(|Y|\le c(X)\)_. The running time of the two algorithms are the same up to a constant factor._

We then obtain the following corollary.

**Corollary B.5** _There is a c-approximation polynomial-time algorithm for the offline version of Problem B.3 iff there is an O(c)-approximation polynomial-time algorithm for the offline_ Min-Sat _problem. Similarly, there is a c-competitive algorithm for the online version of Problem B.3 iff there is a O(c)-competitive algorithm for the online_ Min-Sat _problem._

Let _v_ be the root vertex of _T_ and \(L(v)\in\mathcal{L}\) be vertical line that _v_ owns. Let _T_<sub>1</sub> and _T_<sub>2</sub> be the subtrees of _T_ rooted at the two children of _v_. Notice that _L(v_) partitions the input set _X_ of points into two subsets, _X_<sub>1</sub> and _X_<sub>2</sub>.

We start by adding, for every point \(p\in X\), the point \(p'\), whose _y_-coordinate is _p.y_, and that lies on _L(v_), to the solution _Y_ . We then recursively compute a solution _Y_<sub>1</sub> for _X_<sub>1</sub>, using the partitioning tree _T_<sub>1</sub>, and similarly a solution _Y_<sub>2</sub> for _X_<sub>2</sub>, using the partitioning tree _T_<sub>2</sub>. The final solution is obtained by adding the points of \(Y_1\cup Y_2\) to the set _Y_ . It is easy to verify that _Y_ is indeed a feasible solution. Moreover, each active row of _X_ may contain at most _O_(log_c(X_)) points of _Y_ , and so \(|Y|\le O(r(X)\mathrm{log}c(X))\).

## C.6 Proof of Claim 2.9

It is sufficient to prove that, if _X_ is a semi-permutation, and _T_ is any partitioning tree for _X_, then \(\mathsf{WB}_T(X)\le 2\mathsf{OPT}(X)\).

We prove this claim by induction on the height of _T_. The base case, when the height of _T_ is 0, is obvious: there is only one active column, and so WB_<sub>T</sub>(X_)=OPT(_X_)=0.

We now consider the inductive step. Let _X_ be any point set that is a semi-permutation, and let _T_ be any partitioning tree for _X_, such that the height of _T_ is at least 1. Let _v_ be the root vertex of _T_, _L=L(v_) the line that _v_ owns, and let _v<sub>L</sub>,v<sub>R</sub>_ be the two children of _v_. We assume w.l.o.g. that the strip _S(v<sub>L</sub>_) lies to the left of _S(v<sub>R</sub>_). We denote _S(v_)=_B_ - the bounding box of the instance, _S(v<sub>L</sub>_)=_S<sup>L</sup>,S(v<sub>R</sub>_)=_S<sup>R</sup>_, and we also denote \(X^L=X\cap S^L,X^R=X\cap S^R\). Lastly, we let _T<sup>L</sup>_ and _T<sup>R</sup>_ be the sub-trees of _T_ rooted at _v<sub>L</sub>_ and _v<sub>R</sub>_, respectively. We prove the following claim.

## Claim C.1

\(\mathsf{OPT}(X)\ge\mathsf{OPT}(X^L)+\mathsf{OPT}(X^R)+\mathsf{cost}(v)/2.\)

Notice that, if the claim is correct, then we can use the induction hypothesis on _X<sup>L</sup>_ and _X<sup>R</sup>_ with the trees _T<sup>L</sup>_ and _T<sup>R</sup>_ respectively, to conclude that:

\(\mathsf{OPT}(X)\ge\frac{1}{2}\left(\mathsf{WB}_{T^L}(X_L)+\mathsf{WB}_{T^R}(X_R)+\mathsf{cost}(v)\right)=\frac{1}{2}\mathsf{WB}_T(X).\)

Therefore, in order to complete the proof of Claim 2.9, it is enough to prove Claim C.1.

**Proof of Claim C.1.** Let _Y_ be an optimal solution to instance _X_. We can assume w.l.o.g. that _Y_ is a canonical solution, so no point of _Y_ lies on the line _L_. Let _Y<sup>L</sup>,Y<sup>R</sup>_ be the subsets of points of _Y_ that lie to the left and to the right of the line _L_, respectively.

Let R_<sup>L</sup>_ be the set of all rows _R_, such that (i) no point of _X<sup>L</sup>_ lies on _R_, and (ii) some point of _Y<sup>L</sup>_ lies on _R_. We define a set R_<sup>R</sup>_ of rows similarly for instance _X<sup>R</sup>_. The crux of the proof is the following observation.

**Observation C.2**

\(|\mathcal{R}^L|+|\mathcal{R}^R|\ge\mathsf{cost}(v)/2.\)

Before we prove Observation C.2, we show that Claim C.1 follows from it. In order to do so, we will define a new feasible solution \(\hat{Y}^L\) for instance _X<sup>L</sup>_, containing at most |_Y<sup>L</sup>_|-|R_<sup>L</sup>_| points, and similarly, we will define a new feasible solution \(\hat{Y}^R\) for instance _X<sup>R</sup>_, containing at most |_Y<sup>R</sup>_|-|R_<sup>R</sup>_| points. We now show how to construct the solution \(\hat{Y}^L\) for instance _X<sup>L</sup>_. The solution \(\hat{Y}^R\) for instance _X<sup>R</sup>_ is constructed similarly.

In order to construct the solution \(\hat{Y}^L\), we start with the solution _Y<sup>L</sup>_, and then gradually modify it over the course of |R_<sup>L</sup>_| iterations, where in each iteration we reduce the number of points in the solution _Y<sup>L</sup>_ by at least 1, and we eliminate at most one row from R_<sup>L</sup>_. In order to execute an iteration, we select two rows \(R,R'\), with the following properties:

• Row _R_ contains a point of _X<sup>L</sup>_;<tbc>

• Row \(R'\) contains a point of _Y<sup>L</sup>_ and it contains no points of _X<sup>L</sup>_; and<tbc>

• No point of \(X^L\cup Y^L\) lies strictly between rows _R_ and \(R'\).

Note that, if \(\mathcal{R}^L\neq\emptyset\), such a pair of rows must exist. In order to show this, it is sufficient to show that there must be two points \(p\in R\), \(p'\in R'\) with the same _x_-coordinates; after the two rows are collapsed, these two points are mapped to the same point. Assume for contradiction that no such two points exist. Let \(p\in R\), \(p'\in R'\) be two points with smallest horizontal distance. Then it is easy to see that no point of \(X^L\cup Y^L\) lies in the rectangle \(\square_{p,p^\prime}\), contradicting the fact that _Y<sup>L</sup>_ is a feasible solution for _X<sup>L</sup>_.

In order to complete the proof of Claim C.1, it is now enough to prove Observation C.2.

## D Proof of Lemma 5.3

In this section we prove Lemma 5.3, by showing that for any point set _X_ that is a permutation, \(\mathsf{GB}(X)\le 2\mathsf{OPT}(X)\). In order to do so, it is enough to prove that, for any point set _X_ that is a permutation, for any partitioning tree _T_ for _X_, \(\mathsf{GB}_T(X)\le 2\mathsf{OPT}(X)\). The proof is by induction on the height of _T_, and it is almost identical to the proof of Claim 2.9 for the standard Wilber Bound. When the height of the tree _T_ is 1, then |_X_|=1, so GB(_X_)=0 and OPT(_X_)=0.

Consider now a partitioning tree _T_ whose height is greater than 1. Let _T_<sub>1</sub>_,T_<sub>2</sub> be the two sub-trees of _T_, obtained by deleting the root vertex _r_ from _T_. Let (_X_<sub>1</sub>_,X_<sub>2</sub>) be the partition of _X_ into two subsets given by the line _L(r_), such that _T_<sub>1</sub> is a partitioning tree for _X_<sub>1</sub> and _T_<sub>2</sub> is a partitioning tree for _X_<sub>2</sub>. Notice that, from the definition of the GB bound:

\(\mathsf{GB}_T(X)=\mathsf{GB}_{T_1}(X_1)+\mathsf{GB}_{T_2}(X_2)+\mathsf{cost}(r).\)

Moreover, from the induction hypothesis, \(\mathsf{GB}_{T_1}(X_1)\le 2\mathsf{OPT}(X_1)\) and \(\mathsf{GB}_{T_2}(X_2)\le 2\mathsf{OPT}(X_2)\).

Using Claim C.1 (that can be easily adapted to horizontal partitioning lines), we get that:

\(\mathsf{OPT}(X)\ge\mathsf{OPT}(X_1)+\mathsf{OPT}(X_2)+\mathsf{cost}(r)/2.\)

Therefore, altogether we get that:

\(\mathsf{GB}_T(X)\le 2\mathsf{OPT}(X_1)+2\mathsf{OPT}(X_2)+\mathsf{cost}(r)\le 2\mathsf{OPT}(X).\)
